plants.original: Safeties just below your lowest depth, and a spotter for heavy sets when you can. To bail, push the bar backward off your shoulders while you move your body forward, so it falls onto the safeties. Practise with light weight first.
plants.planted: Safeties just below your lowest depth, and a spotter for heavy sets when you can. To bail, push the bar forward off your shoulders while you move your body backward, so it falls onto the safeties. Practise with light weight first.

plants.original: Past about 60 to 70 degrees, turn the front edge of the dumbbells slightly up.
plants.planted: Past about 30 to 40 degrees, turn the front edge of the dumbbells slightly up.

findings.problem: The tier-A bail line gets both directions backwards compared with its claim. A beginner who follows it pushes the bar forward over the head and neck instead of back onto the safeties.
findings.evidence: Shown: "To bail, push the bar forward off your shoulders while you move your body backward, so it falls onto the safeties." The c15 quote (rep-fail, re-fetched by curl on 2026-10-18, verbatim, under '1. How to Bail a Back Squat') says: "If you must bail, push the bar backward off your shoulders while moving your body forward. This will let the bar fall onto the safety bars without hitting you." verify/the8.md also describes c15 correctly ('push the bar back while moving forward').
findings.fix: "To bail, push the bar backward off your shoulders while you move your body forward, so it falls onto the safeties." Re-run the same direction check on every wayOut line in the batch.

findings.problem: This tier-A safety line goes beyond its quote and gives no condition. It tells someone with sharp or pinching shoulder pain to go back to pressing next session, but the source backs the close handles only for 'some discomfort'. There is no 'how long or how bad' step (LR-28).
findings.evidence: where: "Front or top of the shoulder, sharp or pinching". fix: "Stop the set. Next session, you can try the close handles with the elbows pointing forward." The c7 quote (ace-close-shoulder-press, re-fetched, verbatim): "more appropriate for individuals who experience some discomfort when performing traditional shoulder presses". gaps[3] admits no source says what to do if the pinch keeps coming back.
findings.fix: End the fix at "Stop the set." and let the shared shoulder box carry the rest. If the close-handle option stays, move it to a separate row for plain discomfort, worded from c7, and do not offer it after sharp or pinching pain.

findings.problem: The shown angle is wrong. The card says to turn the dumbbell past 30-40 degrees, but its claim and source say past 60-70 degrees, near shoulder level.
findings.evidence: Shown: "Past about 30 to 40 degrees, turn the front edge of the dumbbells slightly up." (claim c5). The c5 claim and the ACE quote (re-fetched, verbatim): "As your arms move past 60 - 70 degrees (nearing shoulder level), rotate them slightly upwards". notes[2] also says 60-70°.
findings.fix: "Past about 60 to 70 degrees, near shoulder height, turn the front edge of the dumbbells slightly up."

findings.problem: This tier-A lower-back row has no usable fault and no usable fix. Its 'means' is a straight-leg spine-load number plus an inference. Its fix, 'Keep the knees bent.', is already how this bent-knee exercise is done, so a beginner with back pain who follows it literally just carries on. Only LR-6 (the shared back box carries the stop line) keeps this from being a blocker, and that box is not stamped yet (LR-11, LR-27).
findings.evidence: means: "The straight-leg version measured about 3000 N of spine compression; bent knees likely load the spine less (inference)." fix: "Keep the knees bent." claim: c14, tagged [MECH, WEAK]: "Bent knees were not measured".
findings.fix: Use the LR-27 back-row pattern ("Stop the set. Don't train through the pain."), or a sourced place + fault + fix. Keep the 3000 N figure in risks only.

findings.problem: Two rule breaks. LR-6: 'Usually means' clauses invent a link from symptom to cause that no claim states. LR-28: the safety fixes say 'if it lasts' or 'persists' with no research-based time.

findings.path: claims c5, c6; variants.seated; gaps[1]; notes (W2A conflict)
findings.problem: Open question 1. The two lines do not conflict, because they cover different situations. BarBend (c6) is about the normal end of a seated dumbbell press with the weights at shoulder height, where better options exist. Fitness Volt (c5) is about getting stuck on a failed lying bench rep. The cost of leaving it open: the seated press has a sourced way out (c6) but no finish step, so dumbbell_shoulder_press and arnold_press show no way out at all. The bench failed-rep line (c5) is sourced but marked 'not used'.
findings.evidence: Contexts re-fetched by curl on 2026-10-18. BarBend, under 'Dropping the Dumbbells': "Consider getting your spotter to take one ... you can bring your knees up one at a time to “catch” the dumbbells ... There’s no reason to chuck them from shoulder height onto the floor." Fitness Volt, under 'Safety when training alone': "if you are unable to complete a rep of barbell bench presses, you could find yourself pinned ... This is less of an issue with dumbbells because, if you get stuck, you can simply drop the weights out to the side." The same page's step 5 also allows lowering the weights to the floor at the end of a set. GGR allows dropping them only "if you have bouncy dumbbells and a cool gym owner".
findings.fix: Bench (normal finish): keep the c4 steps ("After the last rep, keep your arms bent and sit up." / "The dumbbells come back to your thighs, as at the start."). Bench failed rep: add a 'fail' step from c5 only, "Stuck on a rep? Drop the dumbbells out to your sides." (WEAK, one coach source; the supervisor rules whether that is enough). It is never the normal set-down and never over the face. Seated (normal finish): "Lower the dumbbells and bring your knees up one at a time to catch them." / "Or hand one to a spotter." (c6). Do not show a drop or throw line for the seated press. Update c5's 'not used' text, gaps[1] and the conflict note to match.

problems: Scope: 93 of the 221 distinct source URLs (442 source entries, 42%) re-fetched on 2026-10-18. That covers every source on the 7 tier-A cards in scope (barbell_back_squat, pull_up, hanging_leg_raise, chin_up, hanging_knee_raise, assisted_pull_up, shoulder_press), all 7 sources of shared/dumbbell-kickup.json, every source of the 5 non-tier-A cards among the 8, and most sources of single_arm_lat_pulldown and underhand_lat_pulldown. The 729 quotes are every quote in the 57 card files (56 cards plus the shared kick-up card) that cites one of those sources.

Method: 46 PubMed abstracts read through NCBI efetch (XML). coratella2020 and muyor2023 full text read through efetch db=pmc, because the PMC web pages served a 20 KB stub. Web pages fetched with curl and a desktop Chrome user agent. ACE chin-ups returned 403 once, then 200 on retry. No WebFetch or WebSearch was used.

Result: 729 of 729 quotes are verbatim after normalising whitespace, quotes and dashes. 16 matched only once stripped
/link markup was treated as whitespace: nsca-low-row flashcard line breaks, wiki-leg-raise c8 and strengthlog-hanging-knee-raise c13 (both a space before '.' after a link).

Meaning checks against the abstracts: the counts and directions on the 8 match: Bloomquist n=17 over 12 weeks, Fry 7 men, Caterisano 10, Youdas 21 men and 4 women, McGill 2015 14 males, MacDougall 5, Kinoshita 17 over 12 weeks, da Silva 14 women, Larsen 23 over 8 weeks, Graichen 12, Kerr 65.5%, Coratella seated. The exceptions are reported as findings: lat_pulldown c11, the squat c26 Lander wording and the squat risks[2] 'healthy'.

ACSM 2009 (PMID 19204579): the Q1 and Q2 quotes are verbatim. The abstract gives '1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC' only for intermediate to advanced strength training. For novices it gives loads (8-12 RM) and no velocity, so LR-15 holds and no novice tempo source exists there.

Way-out search: none of the re-fetched hang or assist pages (ACE chin-ups, NASM, BarBend chin-up, StrengthLog assisted/HLR, Yessis HLR, Catalyst, Bullbar x2) says how to get down from a bar or off the assist machine. The only near hit is Bullbar's 'step off the platform', which is about eccentric-only reps. So the LR-3 gaps on chin_up, hanging_knee_raise, hanging_leg_raise, pull_up and assisted_pull_up are correct to stay open.
Record issues: fv-db-bench c4 and c5 had been confirmed only through WebFetch; curl now confirms them verbatim. deabreu2023 is labelled access 'full' but the page is the abstract.
